lines.text: One order, two separate databases. One holds inventory, the other holds the payment.
Both of them have to agree to commit, or neither one should.
Shaking hands on that, across a network, between two machines that don't trust each other blindly, is not the simple part it sounds like.
The first step is a question, not an order.
A coordinator asks every participant one thing. Could you guarantee committing this, if I asked you to right now?
Each one answers only after it's already written down, durably, exactly what it would need to follow through on that guarantee.
Only once every participant has answered yes does the coordinator do something irreversible of its own.
It writes its own decision down, durably, before a single commit message ever goes out.
Only after that does it actually tell everyone involved to commit for real.
Here's where I want you to actually commit to an answer.
The coordinator has been giving every order so far. What happens to the participants if the coordinator itself goes silent, right between those two phases?
You might expect each participant to just give up and decide on its own after a while.
But a participant that already promised it could commit can't safely guess which way to go. Guessing wrong either way could break the whole transaction.
So no. It just sits there, prepared, still holding what it holds, waiting to be told.
Here's that exact prepared state, done for real, against this sandbox's own database.
One session prepares a change and disconnects. A second session looks, and sees nothing has changed yet.
Only a third session, one that never touched this transaction before, is the one that actually commits it.
Now watch what that same prepared transaction is still doing underneath, while it waits.
It's still holding the row it touched. A second, completely separate writer that wants that same row has to wait.
That wait is measured here, for real, and it lasts for exactly as long as that prepared transaction stays unresolved.

lines.text: This is exactly what a real coordinator failure leaves behind.
Locks held. Nothing resolved. For as long as nobody with the authority to decide steps back in.
The database's own documentation is blunt about this. Leave it too long, and it can force a shutdown just to protect itself.
Every production database that does this is really implementing one vendor-neutral standard underneath.
That standard's rule is simple and strict. One single no, from any one participant, vetoes the entire transaction for everyone.
And a yes is never just an optimistic guess. It's a guarantee that committing or rolling back will still work later, even if that participant itself fails in between.
A real distributed database doesn't get to skip this problem. It hides it behind something sturdier instead.
One whole group of machines elects a leader to act as the coordinator. Another whole group elects a leader to act as a participant.
Each one of those leaders is itself backed by its own group reaching agreement, so the fragile single coordinator you just watched become durable, not assumed away.
Pull the whole topic together.
Asking for a guarantee is one phase. Spending that guarantee is the next one.
The gap in between those two phases is real, it's measurable, and shrinking it is most of what a production two-phase-commit implementation actually exists to do.
One last one. A payment and an inventory decrement have to commit together, across two separate databases.
The coordinator process crashes one second after telling both of them to prepare, before either one is ever told to commit.
Given everything you just watched happen in this sandbox. What state are both of those databases actually in right now?
It's tempting to assume a missing commit order just means everything quietly rolls back on its own.
But neither database can safely decide that by itself. Each one already guaranteed it could commit if asked.
So both of them stay exactly where this topic's own measurements left one: prepared, holding their locks, waiting for some session to finally resolve them.
